questions.stem: Before 1905, the Tsarist system of autocracy meant that:
options: the Tsar held supreme power and answered to no elected body
the Tsar shared law-making power with an elected national parliament
the Orthodox Church appointed the Tsar's ministers on his behalf
the zemstvos could veto any law the Tsar proclaimed for their province
questions.explanation: Under autocracy the Tsar's power was unlimited in law: ministers answered to him alone and there was no national parliament before 1906. The zemstvos created in 1864 were local councils with limited powers over matters such as schools and roads, not a check on the Tsar.

questions.stem: Sergei Witte's rapid industrialisation of Russia in the 1890s was financed largely by:
options: the export of manufactured goods to Britain and Germany
indemnity payments that Japan made to Russia after 1905
foreign loans and investment, much of it from France
a heavy new tax on the estates of the landed nobility
questions.explanation: Witte attracted foreign capital, especially French loans, and also relied on high indirect taxes and grain exports, which fell heavily on the peasants. The nobility was not heavily taxed, and Japan paid Russia no indemnity: the 1905 Treaty of Portsmouth ended the war without one.

questions.stem: After the emancipation of the serfs in 1861, many Russian peasants remained resentful mainly because they:
options: were forced to leave the land and move to work in the cities
had to make redemption payments for land they believed was theirs
were still legally owned by the noble landlords of their villages
were forbidden from joining the village commune or mir after 1861
questions.explanation: Emancipation freed peasants legally but obliged them to pay for their allotments over decades, and many received less land than they had worked before. They were no longer owned by landlords, and most stayed bound to the mir, which managed land and collected the payments.

questions.stem: The Battle of Tsushima in May 1905 was:
options: a Russian victory that forced Japan to ask for peace on Russia's terms
the mutiny in which sailors seized the battleship Potemkin off Odessa
a naval disaster in which Russia's fleet sent from the Baltic was destroyed
a land battle that ended the Japanese siege of Port Arthur in Russia's favour
questions.explanation: At Tsushima the Japanese navy destroyed the fleet that had sailed from the Baltic around the world, sealing Russia's defeat. Port Arthur had already fallen to Japan in January 1905, and the Potemkin mutiny was a separate event in the Black Sea that June.

questions.stem: On 9 January 1905, troops fired on a peaceful procession of workers in St Petersburg. The procession was led by:
options: Father Georgi Gapon
Leon Trotsky
Pavel Milyukov
Viktor Chernov
questions.explanation: Gapon, an Orthodox priest who led the police-approved Assembly of Russian Factory Workers, led the march to the Winter Palace. Trotsky became prominent later in 1905 in the St Petersburg Soviet; Milyukov was a liberal leader and Chernov led the Socialist Revolutionaries.

questions.stem: The petition carried by the marchers on Bloody Sunday asked the Tsar for:
options: an immediate alliance with Japan against Britain and France
an eight-hour day and a constituent assembly elected by all
the abolition of the monarchy and the creation of a republic
the transfer of all noble estates to the Social Democrats
questions.explanation: The petition was loyal in tone, appealing to the Tsar for justice, and its demands included an eight-hour day, civil freedoms and a constituent assembly. It did not seek to abolish the monarchy, which is why the shooting so badly damaged the marchers' faith in the Tsar.

questions.stem: The mutiny on the battleship Potemkin in June 1905 was significant because it showed that:
options: the Black Sea Fleet was firmly under the control of the Bolshevik party
the navy was the most loyal pillar of the autocracy during the war
Japan had begun landing troops in Russia's southern Black Sea ports
the armed forces could not always be relied on to defend the regime
questions.explanation: The regime's survival depended on the loyalty of soldiers and sailors, so a mutiny in a major warship was alarming even though it was contained. The mutineers were not directed by the Bolsheviks, and Japan never landed troops on the Black Sea coast.

questions.stem: The October Manifesto of 1905 promised:
options: the immediate transfer of all noble land to the peasant communes
an eight-hour working day in every factory throughout the empire
civil liberties and an elected Duma whose consent was needed for laws
a republic with an elected president and a cabinet chosen by the Duma
questions.explanation: Drafted with Witte's advice during the general strike, the Manifesto promised freedoms of conscience, speech, assembly and association, a wider franchise, and that no law would take effect without the Duma's approval. It kept the monarchy and did not grant land or an eight-hour day.

questions.stem: Historians often argue that the October Manifesto helped the Tsarist regime survive 1905. The best reason is that it:
options: split moderate liberals who accepted it from socialists who rejected it
persuaded the Bolsheviks and Mensheviks to reunite as a single party
gave the soviets a guaranteed and permanent role in the government
allowed the Tsar to win the war against Japan in the months after
questions.explanation: Many liberals, such as the future Octobrists, accepted the Manifesto, while socialists kept up the struggle; this division let the government isolate and crush the St Petersburg and Moscow soviets in December. The war had already ended in September 1905, in defeat.

questions.stem: A student argues that the Fundamental Laws of April 1906 honoured the October Manifesto's promises. Which feature of the Laws best challenges this argument?
options: They gave the Duma control over foreign policy and the armed forces
They declared that supreme autocratic power still belonged to the Tsar
They abolished the Duma before its first session was able to meet
They made the Tsar's ministers responsible to the elected Duma
questions.explanation: The Fundamental Laws reasserted that the Emperor held supreme autocratic power and kept ministers, the army and foreign policy under his control, with an appointed State Council as an upper house. The first Duma did meet in April 1906, so the Laws limited the Duma rather than abolished it.

questions.stem: After the first two Dumas were dissolved, the government changed the electoral law in June 1907 so that:
options: landowners and the wealthy gained far greater weight in elections
all adult men and women could vote by direct secret ballot
peasants elected a clear majority of deputies directly
only socialist parties could stand candidates in the large industrial cities
questions.explanation: The June 1907 law, often called Stolypin's coup, cut the representation of peasants, workers and national minorities and favoured landowners, producing a more conservative Third Duma. It narrowed rather than widened the franchise.

questions.stem: Stolypin's agrarian reforms from 1906 aimed mainly to:
options: collectivise peasant farms into large estates run by the state
transfer the estates of the nobility to landless rural labourers
create a class of prosperous peasant landowners loyal to the regime
return the land seized by peasants in 1905 to the village communes
questions.explanation: Stolypin's 'wager on the strong' let peasants leave the commune and consolidate their strips into private farms, hoping a contented landowning peasantry would be a conservative force. The reforms left noble estates intact and had nothing to do with collectivisation, which came under Stalin.

questions.stem: A historian describes Stolypin's policy as 'repression and reform'. Which pairing best fits that description?
options: Abolition of the Okhrana; nationalisation of large-scale industry
Universal male suffrage for the Duma; collectivisation of farms
Exile of Rasputin to Siberia; abolition of the zemstvo councils
Field courts-martial for rebels; land consolidation for peasants
questions.explanation: Stolypin crushed unrest with summary courts while offering peasants the chance to own consolidated farms. He strengthened rather than abolished the police, narrowed the Duma franchise in 1907, and collectivisation was a Soviet policy.

questions.stem: Nicholas II's decision in 1915 to take personal command of the army damaged the monarchy mainly because:
options: he was now held personally responsible for military defeats
it left the army without any officers of noble background
it forced the Duma to withdraw its support for the war
it required the capital to be moved from Petrograd to Moscow
questions.explanation: At headquarters in Mogilev, Nicholas became directly linked to every defeat and shortage, and he left government in Petrograd to Alexandra. The capital stayed in Petrograd until the Bolsheviks moved it to Moscow in 1918.

questions.stem: While Nicholas was at army headquarters from 1915, Alexandra's role in government was widely resented chiefly because she:
options: ordered the army to fire on the striking Putilov workers
repeatedly replaced ministers, often on Rasputin's advice
negotiated a secret separate peace with the German Kaiser
transferred the Tsar's powers to the Progressive Bloc
questions.explanation: Frequent changes of ministers, known as 'ministerial leapfrog', and Rasputin's apparent influence discredited the government; even monarchist nobles murdered Rasputin in December 1916 to save the dynasty's name. Rumours that the German-born Empress was a traitor were false: she negotiated no peace with Germany.

questions.stem: By the winter of 1916–17, Petrograd suffered severe food shortages even though Russia was still producing grain. The main reasons were:
options: a Duma law banning the sale of bread in the capital in wartime
overloaded railways and peasants holding grain back from market
a British naval blockade of Russia's Black Sea and Baltic ports
the Tsar's order that most grain be exported to pay war debts
questions.explanation: The railways were overwhelmed by military traffic, and inflation and the lack of manufactured goods led peasants to hold back grain. Britain was Russia's ally, not its blockader; it was Germany and Turkey that cut Russia's sea routes.

questions.stem: In November 1916 Pavel Milyukov listed the government's failures in the Duma, repeatedly asking 'Is this stupidity or is it treason?' His speech is best used as evidence that:
options: the Kadets wanted Russia to withdraw from the war
Milyukov supported Rasputin's influence at court
liberals had lost confidence in the Tsar's government
the Bolsheviks controlled a majority in the Fourth Duma
questions.explanation: Milyukov, the Kadet leader, accused the government of incompetence or worse, showing that even moderate liberals had turned against it. The Kadets wanted to win the war, not leave it, and the Bolsheviks had only a handful of Duma deputies.

questions.stem: The February Revolution began on 23 February 1917 with:
options: the dissolution of the Duma by the Tsar's ministers
International Women's Day protests over bread in Petrograd
a Bolshevik seizure of the Winter Palace and the Duma
a mutiny by sailors of the Baltic Fleet at the Kronstadt naval base
questions.explanation: Women textile workers and housewives queuing for bread marched on International Women's Day, and the protests spread into a general strike. The Bolsheviks did not lead the February rising, and the Winter Palace was taken only in October.

questions.stem: The decisive turning point of the February Revolution came on 27 February 1917 when:
options: Lenin arrived at the Finland Station and addressed the workers
Kerensky ordered the arrest of the Tsar and his ministers
the Bolsheviks won a majority in the Petrograd Soviet
soldiers of the Petrograd garrison mutinied and joined the crowds
questions.explanation: Once regiments such as the Volynsky refused to fire and went over to the protesters, the government had no force to restore order. Lenin was still in Switzerland, and the Bolsheviks gained a Soviet majority only in September.

questions.stem: On 26 February 1917 the Duma President, Rodzianko, telegraphed Nicholas that there was anarchy in the capital and the government was paralysed. Nicholas dismissed the warning. The best inference from this is that:
options: Rodzianko was calling on the Tsar to hand power to the Bolsheviks
the Duma had already deposed the Tsar before the telegram was sent
the army had restored order in Petrograd by the time it was read
the Tsar misjudged how serious the crisis in Petrograd had become
questions.explanation: Rodzianko, a monarchist, urged the Tsar to appoint a government with public confidence; Nicholas instead ordered the disorders suppressed, and within days the garrison mutinied. The source shows the gap between the Tsar's view and events, not any Bolshevik sympathy in the Duma.

questions.stem: The Dual Authority (dvoevlastie) of 1917 refers to power shared between:
options: the Tsar and the Fourth State Duma
the Bolsheviks and the Mensheviks
the Council of People's Commissars and the Constituent Assembly
the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet
questions.explanation: After February the Provisional Government had formal authority, but the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies commanded the loyalty of workers and the garrison. The Sovnarkom was created only after October.

questions.stem: Order No. 1 of the Petrograd Soviet (1 March 1917) told soldiers to obey the Provisional Government's military orders only if they did not conflict with the Soviet's. Its main significance was that it:
options: placed the army under the personal command of Lenin
ordered the army to stop fighting Germany at once
made the Provisional Government the sole legal power
gave the Soviet a decisive hold over the armed forces
questions.explanation: By making the Soviet the final authority for soldiers, Order No. 1 meant the Provisional Government could not rely on the army, which lay at the heart of the Dual Authority. It did not end the war, and Lenin was not yet in Russia.

questions.stem: In April 1917 Foreign Minister Milyukov's note to the Allies provoked street protests and led to his resignation. The note had promised that:
options: Russia would give up its claims on Constantinople
Russia would fight on until a decisive victory
Russia would sign a separate peace with Germany
the Tsar would be restored as a constitutional monarch
questions.explanation: The Soviet had called for peace without annexations, so Milyukov's pledge to fight to victory and honour the old war aims caused the April Crisis. A coalition with Soviet socialists followed, which tied them to the government's failures.

questions.stem: After the July Days of 1917, the Bolsheviks' position weakened because:
options: they had lost all of their seats in the newly elected Constituent Assembly
they were accused of being German agents and Lenin fled to Finland
they had joined the Provisional Government and were blamed for the war
Kornilov's troops had executed most of the party's Central Committee
questions.explanation: The government published claims that Lenin was in German pay, arrested leading Bolsheviks including Trotsky, and Lenin went into hiding in Finland. The Bolsheviks never joined the Provisional Government, and the Constituent Assembly was elected only in November.

questions.stem: The Kornilov Affair of August 1917 helped the Bolsheviks mainly because:
options: Kornilov's victory forced Kerensky to invite Lenin to join his coalition cabinet
it ended the war with Germany and freed the soldiers to join the Bolsheviks
the Tsar was briefly restored and then overthrown by the Bolsheviks alone
the Red Guards were armed and the Bolsheviks seemed defenders of the revolution
questions.explanation: Facing a feared military coup, Kerensky turned to the Soviet, released Bolshevik prisoners and let the Red Guards be armed; Kornilov's advance collapsed. Kerensky was discredited on both left and right, while the Bolsheviks gained credit and support.

questions.stem: By early September 1917 the Bolsheviks held majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets, and Trotsky soon became chairman of the Petrograd Soviet. Which event most directly preceded this shift?
options: The April Crisis
The February Revolution
The Kornilov Affair
The July Days
questions.explanation: The Bolshevik surge in the soviets followed directly from the Kornilov Affair at the end of August. The July Days had the opposite effect, leaving the party accused of treason, its press shut down and Lenin in hiding.

questions.stem: In his April Theses, Lenin called for:
options: the return of the monarchy under Grand Duke Michael as constitutional Tsar
no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets
cooperation with the Provisional Government until the war was won
a long period of bourgeois democracy before any socialist revolution
questions.explanation: The April Theses rejected the Provisional Government, demanded an end to the war, transfer of power to the soviets and confiscation of landed estates. This broke with the cautious line of Bolsheviks in Petrograd who had been giving the government conditional support.

questions.stem: Leading Bolsheviks in Petrograd, including Kamenev, at first opposed the April Theses. The main reason was that Lenin was:
options: abandoning Marxism for the Socialist Revolutionaries' programme
calling for Russia to keep fighting alongside Britain and France
proposing that the Bolsheviks merge with the Kadet party
rejecting the view that a long bourgeois stage must come first
questions.explanation: Orthodox Marxism held that the bourgeois revolution of February had to run its course before a socialist one; Kamenev wrote in Pravda that the Theses were Lenin's personal view. Lenin demanded peace, so he was not calling for the war to continue.

questions.stem: The body that planned and carried out the Bolshevik seizure of power in Petrograd in October 1917 was:
options: the Progressive Bloc of liberal deputies in the Fourth State Duma
the Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet
the defence committee of the Constituent Assembly
the Cheka, the new Soviet political police force
questions.explanation: The Military Revolutionary Committee, set up by the Petrograd Soviet and directed in practice by Trotsky, organised the seizure of key points on 24–25 October. The Cheka was founded only in December 1917.

questions.stem: At the Bolshevik Central Committee meeting of 10 October 1917, which two leaders voted against Lenin's call for an armed rising and then made their opposition public?
options: Zinoviev and Kamenev
Trotsky and Sverdlov
Stalin and Dzerzhinsky
Martov and Dan
questions.explanation: The Central Committee voted ten to two for insurrection; Zinoviev and Kamenev argued it was premature and published their objections in a non-party paper. Martov and Dan were Menshevik leaders, not members of the Bolshevik Central Committee.

questions.stem: Trotsky's main contribution to the October 1917 seizure of power was:
options: persuading the Kadets to vote for the transfer of power to the soviets
commanding the Red Army as it defeated the White generals in the south
signing the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk to free troops for the insurrection
organising the rising through the Military Revolutionary Committee
questions.explanation: As chairman of the Petrograd Soviet, Trotsky used the Military Revolutionary Committee to win over the garrison and time the rising for the Congress of Soviets. His Red Army command and the peace negotiations came after October.

questions.stem: When the Second Congress of Soviets opened on 25 October 1917, most Mensheviks and Right SRs walked out in protest at the rising. The most significant consequence was that:
options: Kerensky was elected chairman of the Council of People's Commissars
the Congress was abandoned and Soviet power was never formally declared
the Bolsheviks and Left SRs were left to approve the new Soviet government
the Congress voted to restore the Provisional Government under Kerensky
questions.explanation: The walkout removed the main opposition, and the remaining Bolsheviks and Left SRs endorsed Soviet power, the decrees on peace and land and a Sovnarkom chaired by Lenin on 26 October. Trotsky told those leaving that they belonged in the 'dustbin of history'.

questions.stem: According to Marx, history moves through a series of stages driven by:
options: conflict between social classes
the will of great individual leaders
the decisions of religious authorities
the conquests of foreign empires
questions.explanation: Marx's historical materialism held that struggle between classes over the means of production drives change, from feudalism to capitalism and then to socialism. Lenin added the role of a vanguard party, but class struggle remained the engine of history.

questions.stem: Lenin's version of Marxism differed from orthodox Marxism mainly in arguing that:
options: a disciplined vanguard party must lead the workers to revolution
revolution would come first in the most advanced capitalist country
capitalism could be reformed into socialism through elections
the nobility would lead the workers in overthrowing capitalism
questions.explanation: In What Is to Be Done? (1902) Lenin argued that workers left to themselves would develop only trade-union consciousness, so a party of professional revolutionaries must lead them. Revolution in the most advanced capitalist country was Marx's own expectation, not Lenin's innovation.

questions.stem: At the 1903 Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, Lenin and Martov split most fundamentally over:
options: whether the party should seek an alliance with the Japanese government
whether the party should support the Tsar's war against Turkey
whether the party should accept Marx's theory of class struggle
whether party membership should be limited to active revolutionaries
questions.explanation: Lenin wanted a narrow party of committed professional revolutionaries, while Martov wanted a broader membership; Lenin's faction took the name Bolsheviks (majority) and Martov's became the Mensheviks (minority). Both factions accepted class struggle as Marxists.

questions.stem: Many Mensheviks supported the Provisional Government in 1917 because they believed that:
options: Lenin's party was the true vanguard of the Russian working class
Russia had to pass through a bourgeois capitalist stage before socialism
the Tsar should be restored as a constitutional monarch under the Duma
only the peasant communes could carry out a true socialist revolution
questions.explanation: Following orthodox Marxism, Mensheviks saw February as a bourgeois revolution that socialists should not try to cut short, so they backed the government and later joined it. The belief that the peasant commune could be the basis of socialism belonged to the Socialist Revolutionaries.

questions.stem: The Socialist Revolutionaries drew most of their support from:
options: the nobility and army officers
Moscow's business community
the peasantry
factory workers in the cities
questions.explanation: The SRs, led by Viktor Chernov, demanded that land be given to those who worked it, which made them the largest party among the peasants. They won the most seats in the Constituent Assembly elections of November 1917.

questions.stem: Richard Pipes described October 1917 as a classic coup d'état. Which evidence would a historian who sees October as a revolution from below most likely stress?
options: The secrecy with which the Military Revolutionary Committee laid its plans
Bolshevik majorities in the soviets reflected workers' and soldiers' radicalism
The small number of armed men who took part in seizing the Winter Palace
Lenin's insistence that the Central Committee act before the Congress met
questions.explanation: Historians who stress popular radicalism point to growing support for Soviet power in the factories, garrison and soviets by autumn 1917. The small numbers involved, Lenin's urgency and the secret planning are the evidence Pipes used for a coup by a conspiratorial minority.

questions.stem: Alexander Rabinowitch, in The Bolsheviks Come to Power, argued that the Bolsheviks took power in Petrograd largely because:
options: German money allowed them to buy the loyalty of the city garrison
the Provisional Government handed them power without resistance
their flexible organisation and policies won genuine popular support
a tightly controlled elite seized power against the people's wishes
questions.explanation: Rabinowitch found that the Bolshevik party in Petrograd in 1917 was relatively open and responsive, and that its slogans matched the aims of workers and soldiers. The view of a conspiratorial elite acting against the people is associated with Pipes, which Rabinowitch's research challenged.

questions.stem: Orlando Figes called his history of the revolution A People's Tragedy. His interpretation emphasises:
options: ordinary people's part in a revolution that ended in dictatorship
the inevitable triumph of the working class under Lenin's guidance
a revolution caused almost entirely by German secret operations
the Tsar's success in modernising Russia before the war began
questions.explanation: Figes stresses the hopes and actions of peasants, workers and soldiers, while arguing that the revolution they helped make went on to destroy them. The idea of an inevitable proletarian triumph is the official Soviet interpretation, which Figes rejects.

questions.stem: Official Soviet historians presented October 1917 as:
options: a coup by a small conspiratorial minority acting against the will of the people
an accident caused by the personal weakness of Alexander Kerensky
a revolt of the nobility against Nicholas II's wartime failures
a mass proletarian revolution led by Lenin's party, as history required
questions.explanation: The Soviet interpretation saw October as the lawful outcome of class struggle, with the Bolsheviks leading the workers and poorest peasants. The minority-coup view was held by Western liberal historians such as Pipes.
